hero.title: The Fog Is Lifting
hero.lead: Whether you're curious about Islam, have pressing questions, seek interesting facts about Islam and the Quran, or are looking for an accurate Quran translation, The Fog Is Lifting is here to guide you.

toc.title: The collection
toc.subtitle: Documentaries, short series, books, and a course — arranged as a quiet reading room rather than a feed.

islamInBrief.title: Islam in Brief
body: In the first part of The Fog Is Lifting, “Islam in Brief”, you will learn in 74 minutes more about Islamic beliefs and rituals than you can acquire in 74 days of reading.
For the viewer’s convenience, the film consists of ten chapters; each one deals with a specific concept, belief or ritual. Watching the chapters in order is recommended.
Islam in Brief began as a presentation given by Fadel Soliman — the author of the film — to over 40,000 non-Muslims around the world: in churches, universities, conferences and government agencies.

jihadOnTerrorism.title: Jihad on Terrorism
body: As the second part of The Fog Is Lifting, “Jihad on Terrorism” tackles the most controversial misconception spread in the West after 9/11: that Islam is the religion of terrorists, and that the Quran is a book of violence and hatred.

Through this 100-minute Bridges Foundation documentary you will learn the true meaning of “Jihad”: that Islam gave people a way to end terror in the world, and that jihad is the true war on terrorism.

islamInWomen.title: Islam in Women
body: Islam in Women examines a striking fact: a majority of new converts to Islam are women, even though many Islamophobic attacks claim that Islam is discriminatory and oppressive toward women.

Through candid interviews with twelve female converts — including a non-Muslim woman, a professor from Al-Azhar University, and a professor at Harvard Divinity School — the film reveals why the religion attracts more women than men, and refutes common misconceptions.
The women hail from Belgium, Britain, Germany, Greece, Hong Kong, Indonesia, the Netherlands, Sri Lanka, Sweden and the United States.

islamophobia1.lead: A 29-part YouTube series answering questions and debunking misconceptions about Islam, Muslims, Sharia, Muslim life, and the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him).
questions: Is religion the opiate of the masses?
How could a prophet of God raid a caravan?
Muhammad and Aisha: the perfect love story
Why do Muslim women wear hijab?
How did Islam deal with slavery?
Does Islam forbid friendship with non-Muslims?
Can a Muslim be an actor or a musician?
Are women oppressed by Islam?
Is it true that ex-Muslims should be killed?
All of this — and more — in the playlist.

doNotHate.title: Don't Hate, Educate
doNotHate.lead: In less than half an hour, across 30 short YouTube videos, discover the life and teachings of Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him): his personality, manners, and way of living.

islamophobia2.kicker: Do you find yourself pondering life's profound questions?

inventions.title: 1001 Inventions: The Enduring Legacy of Muslim Civilization
body: 1001 Inventions takes readers through forgotten Islamic history to discover scientific and technological inventions still used throughout the world today — engineering, early medicine, and the origins of cartography among them.
The book covers seven aspects of life: home, school, hospital, market, town, world and universe.
inventions.explore: Explore more at 1001inventions.com and the 1001 Inventions YouTube channel.

inventionsKids.title: 1001 Inventions and Awesome Facts from Muslim Civilization
inventionsKids.imageAlt: Cover of the children's companion to 1001 Inventions
body: From the 7th century onward, Muslim civilization produced advances that still shape everyday life: water clocks, detailed maps, universities founded by women, vast domes, and charts of the stars.
This National Geographic companion packs facts, photographs and stories that connect that history to the world children live in now.

science.title: Science and the Holy Quran
science.imageAlt: Artwork for Science and the Quran
science.quote: “We will show them Our signs in the universe and in their own selves, until it becomes manifest to them that this (the Quran) is the truth.” (Quran 41:53)
body: The Quran is not a scientific textbook, yet it contains remarkable insights that reach beyond science. Some people exaggerate supposed ‘scientific miracles’; still, there are undeniably fascinating observations.
How could an illiterate man living in the desert more than fourteen centuries ago mention phenomena discovered by modern science only in the last century?
science.article: 13 scientific facts in the Holy Quran
science.video: The many scientific miracles of the Holy Quran

philosophy.title: The Story of Faith between Philosophy, Science, and the Qur'an
philosophy.imageAlt: Cover of The Story of Faith
body: Hayran Ibn al-Ad'af is a young man whose passion for philosophy leads him to search for answers after being expelled from school. His notebook records the discussions of Sheikh Abu An-Nur al-Mawzun of Samarqand.

Sheikh Nadim al-Jisr, Mufti of Tripoli and Northern Lebanon, presents those answers without narrowing them to slogans: Greek, Muslim and Western thought, and what the Qur'an evokes toward faith and certainty.
philosophy.audio: If you know Arabic, do not miss the immersive audio version on the Bridges Foundation YouTube channel.

translation.title: Bridges' Translation of the Ten Qira'at of the Noble Qur'an
translation.imageAlt: Cover of Bridges' Translation of the Qur'an
translation.lead: Bridges’ translation helps the non-Arabic reader ponder the Qur’an (tadabbur). The translators focused not only on what God meant to say, but on how He spoke.
features: It is the first translation that includes the ten Qira’at (modes of recitation). The main text follows Asem, narrated by Hafs. About 30% of the variations — those that affect meaning — appear in footnotes.
It is the first translation that respects Qur’anic grammatical shifts in verb tenses, numbers, and pronouns. Speaking about the Hereafter in the past tense is kept.
Singular, dual and plural forms of pronouns and imperative verbs are marked with superscripts (youpl, yousg, youdl) rather than inserted interpretations in brackets.
